topics.title: 48.1 Waiting
topics.summary: Waiting should mean “sleep until it is worth checking the predicate again,” not “assume the event must have happened because I woke up.” A waiter holds the mutex while inspecting state and uses the condition variable to release ownership while blocked. This avoids wasting CPU in a polling loop and allows the producer of the condition to acquire the mutex. Waiting while continuing to hold the needed mutex would prevent the state change that could satisfy the predicate.

topics.title: 48.2 Notification
topics.summary: Notification makes one or more waiters eligible to reconsider their predicates. It does not transfer the mutex directly into a guarantee that the predicate remains true until the awakened thread runs. Another thread may acquire the mutex first and consume the resource. The waiter must therefore recheck under the lock. Notification is a scheduling hint within a state protocol, not the protocol’s authoritative record.

topics.title: 48.3 wait
topics.summary: wait atomically releases the associated lock and enters the waiting operation, then reacquires the lock before returning to the caller. The predicate overload expresses the required loop directly. Use the same mutex discipline for the predicate’s shared state. Updating the predicate without its required protection can introduce a data race or lose the relationship between state change and sleeping. The mutex and condition variable must remain alive while waiters can use them.

topics.title: 48.4 notify_one
topics.summary: notify_one wakes one eligible waiter. It is appropriate when one newly available unit of work can satisfy one interchangeable consumer. The awakened thread still competes for the mutex and checks the predicate. When different waiter classes use different predicates, waking an arbitrary one may not produce progress. Separate condition variables or broader notification may be needed. Choose based on the state machine, not solely on a desire to minimize wakeups.

topics.title: 48.5 notify_all
topics.summary: notify_all wakes all current waiters so that each can check its condition. It is useful for closure, shutdown, or state changes that may satisfy several different predicates. Waking many threads can create contention, sometimes called a thundering herd. That cost does not justify omitting required wakeups. First ensure all affected waiters can make progress or terminate; then refine the notification policy if measurement shows a problem.

topics.title: 48.6 Predicate loops
topics.summary: A predicate loop handles spurious wakeups and state changes consumed by another participant. The canonical form is condition.wait(lock, [&]{ return predicate; }); . After it returns, the predicate is true while the caller still owns the mutex. Do not move the predicate check outside the lock to save a few instructions. The check and decision to wait must be coordinated with the state updates. An atomic flag alone does not automatically repair a poorly designed condition-variable protocol.

topics.title: 48.8 Lost wakeups
topics.summary: A notification sent when no thread is waiting is not retained as a future wakeup token. This is harmless when the state predicate remains true: a later waiter sees it and does not sleep. It is a bug only when the design incorrectly relies on notification history instead of persistent state. For example, set ready = true under the mutex, then notify. A worker that starts after the notification still observes ready and proceeds. Omitting the state variable and waiting for an imagined remembered notification is the broken design.
